sections.authorBiography: Nathaniel Hawthorne was born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 4 July 1804; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge in the Salem witch trials of 1692, a family history Hawthorne felt as a burden. He later changed the spelling of his surname to Hawthorne; why is uncertain, though many link it to his discomfort with his ancestors. After graduating from Bowdoin College in 1825 he spent years writing in near-seclusion in Salem, publishing Twice-Told Tales in 1837. He lived briefly at the utopian Brook Farm community, worked at the Salem Custom House, and achieved fame with The Scarlet Letter (1850) and The House of the Seven Gables (1851). He served as U.S. consul in Liverpool and died on 19 May 1864 in Plymouth, New Hampshire.
sections.historicalContext: The novel is set in Puritan Boston in the 1640s, about twenty years after the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Colony (1630). The Puritan colony joined church and civil authority: magistrates punished moral offenses such as adultery publicly, and colonial laws allowed for punishments including whipping, the pillory and, in some periods, the wearing of letters. Real figures appear: Governor Richard Bellingham, the minister John Wilson, Mistress Ann Hibbins (executed for witchcraft in 1656) and Governor John Winthrop, whose death in 1649 coincides with the minister's vigil. Hawthorne wrote two centuries later, in 1849, after losing his post as surveyor of the Salem Custom House when the Whigs won the presidency; he writes of that dismissal in "The Customhouse."

publicationAndReception.publication: Ticknor, Reed and Fields of Boston published The Scarlet Letter in March 1850, with "The Customhouse" as an introductory sketch. A second edition followed within weeks; Hawthorne's "Preface to the Second Edition" (dated 30 March 1850) refuses to change the sketch despite local anger. By Fields's own later account, he persuaded Hawthorne to publish the story as a separate volume rather than in a planned collection of tales.
publicationAndReception.then: The book sold well quickly, and the first printing sold out within days. Reviewers praised its power and artistry; some religious critics, such as Arthur Cleveland Coxe, condemned it as an immoral book about adultery. Salem readers resented the satirical portraits of Custom House officers.
publicationAndReception.now: The Scarlet Letter is among the most taught novels in American high schools and is usually called the first great American novel of psychological and moral analysis. It has been filmed several times (including a 1926 silent film with Lillian Gish and a 1995 film), retold and parodied, and the phrase "scarlet letter" has entered English for any public mark of shame. Modern readers discuss Hester as a feminist figure, the ethics of public shaming, and Hawthorne's own ambivalence toward his Puritan ancestors.

sections.overview: In seventeenth-century Boston, a young woman named Hester Prynne stands on a scaffold holding a baby, with a scarlet "A" embroidered on her dress. She refuses to name the baby's father. The novel follows Hester, her daughter Pearl, the community that judges her, and two men whose connection to her the town does not know.

spoilerOverview.text: The father is the young, revered minister Arthur Dimmesdale. Hester's long-absent husband arrives the day she is shamed, takes the name Roger Chillingworth, and as a physician attaches himself to Dimmesdale, whose guilt is wasting him, and torments him. Seven years later Hester meets Dimmesdale in the forest and they plan to flee to Europe; Chillingworth books passage on the same ship. After his Election Sermon, Dimmesdale mounts the scaffold with Hester and Pearl, confesses, reveals something on his breast, and dies. Chillingworth dies within a year and leaves his fortune to Pearl, who goes abroad and marries. Hester later returns to Boston, wears the letter of her own will, counsels women, and is buried near Dimmesdale under one tombstone with the words "On a field, sable, the letter A, gules."

Whether Massachusetts Bay actually sentenced adulterers to wear a letter in the 1640s is not certain; a 1694 Massachusetts law and a 1658 Plymouth law prescribed letters. Present the letter as Hawthorne's use of colonial practice, not as a documented 1640s sentence.
The claim that Hawthorne added the "w" to his surname to distance himself from his ancestors is common but not documented in his own words; present it as a widely held view.
Fields's role in persuading Hawthorne to publish the story alone comes from Fields's later memoir (Yesterdays with Authors, 1872); treat it as his account.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this chapter, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in The Scarlet Letter.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about The Scarlet Letter: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

collegeSenior.label: College Senior
collegeSenior.text: Write a research paper (12–15 pages) with an original argument about women and independence in The Scarlet Letter, engaging at least four scholarly sources in Chicago style. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on women and independence in The Scarlet Letter, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history. At this level students write ONE of the unit's essays (choose one theme), not all five.

finalPaper.title: The Scarlet Letter: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how Nathaniel Hawthorne develops sin and guilt across The Scarlet Letter. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in The Scarlet Letter and argue how its meaning changes over the novel and why that change matters to public shame and private identity.
Analyze a central character's choices in The Scarlet Letter. Argue whether the novel judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.

Two readers disagree about whether The Scarlet Letter finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of hypocrisy and truth. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the chapter and paragraph (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

criticalVoices.quote: _The Scarlet Letter_ has the beauty and harmony of all original and complete conceptions, and its weaker spots, whatever they are, are not of its essence; they are mere light flaws and inequalities of surface.
criticalVoices.speaker: Henry James, novelist and critic
criticalVoices.source: Hawthorne (English Men of Letters, 1879), Chapter V, Ch. V
criticalVoices.useNote: Closure: name one "light flaw" you found and argue it is not "of its essence."
criticalVoices.linkedObjective: Closing lesson: evaluate the novel's lasting value.
